question: What exactly is being priced — the full-game winner, the spread, the total, or a specific prop — and for which market type first?
why_it_matters: Every downstream choice (data needed, sample size, validation test) differs by market. A spread needs a margin model; a winner market needs only a probability. A total needs a pace model. Picking all of them at once guarantees none reaches statistical significance this season.
what_we_know: The brief asks for single bets, parlays and player-prop combos. Official NFL data supplies team scoring (PF/PA), records and game status, which is enough to specify a spread or total model.
what_we_dont_know: Which market the user wants first, and whether the goal is to beat a specific book's price or to produce an independent fair-value number.
missing_data: A target market. A benchmark price source to compare against.
recommended_path: Start with a single market we can fully specify from official data (team spread), reach a validated result, then extend. Do not start with parlays: they multiply variance and hide which leg failed.
answer: Side first — the order is pre-registered: originate the side, then the total, then the moneyline (data/origination_order.json; brief audit D-03). model_lines.tsv prints the step order on every row ('1 side > 2 total > 3 moneyline') and publishes fair, market and difference as separate columns per market (D-04). The side is the anchor quantity: both other markets are downstream of the same scoring decomposition.

question: Is the objective a single published line per game, or a repeatable pipeline that regenerates lines weekly?
why_it_matters: A one-off line cannot be validated. Only a pipeline that emits a number before kickoff, for many games, produces a record that can be judged against outcomes.
what_we_know: Official NFL schedules give kickoff times and matchups, so a pre-kickoff timestamp can be attached to every generated line.
what_we_dont_know: Whether the user wants historical backtesting, live forward-testing, or both.
missing_data: Historical closing lines and results to backtest against are not present in this repository and are not published as a bulk official dataset by the NFL.
recommended_path: Forward-testing with a sealed, timestamped record. Every prediction is written to disk before kickoff with a hash, so results cannot be edited afterwards.
answer: A repeatable pipeline. Every published line is regenerated from committed inputs on each rebuild (tools/build.py -> scripts/build_fair_lines_m.py -> data/model_lines.tsv and data/fair_lines.csv), and every row carries its model version and market provenance. One fair line per game per market at a time is the pipeline's scheduled output — not a hand-entry.

question: What is the official source for a *market* price to measure our own line against?
why_it_matters: Without a benchmark price there is no way to compute edge, closing-line value, or whether a strategy is profitable. A strategy graded only on 'did it win' cannot separate skill from luck.
what_we_know: Official league sources publish results, stats and schedules, but not betting prices. Sportsbook prices are commercial data.
what_we_dont_know: Which price source the user will accept as the benchmark, and whether they have access to one.
missing_data: A licensed or user-supplied odds feed. Nothing of the kind exists in this repo.
recommended_path: Do not invent prices. Until a benchmark feed is supplied, output only a fair-value probability and a stated uncertainty, and grade strategies on calibration (predicted vs realised) rather than profit.
answer: No official league source publishes betting prices; the board records this as GAP-01 and leaves market cells blank with the reason (model_lines.tsv market_status; F18). Market values that do appear come from a third-party feed and are labelled per row (market_provenance in data/fair_lines.csv). The open half is approval of a market-price source for headline numbers (Q21, Q30, Q32; D-20).

question: Is there an official league-wide depth chart, or must depth come from each of the 32 club sites?
why_it_matters: The brief asks which 2nd/3rd/4th-string players are replacing starters. Ranking depth requires a depth ordering. If there is no league-wide feed, the build is 32 separate scrapers with 32 different formats, and inconsistency becomes the main error source.
what_we_know: https://www.nfl.com/depth-charts/ returns 404 (S13). Individual club sites do publish depth charts, and the Chiefs page is explicitly titled 'Unofficial Depth Chart' (S08). NFL.com rosters do carry a status code (ACT/RES/CUT/DEV/PUP/TRD) per player (S07).
what_we_dont_know: Whether every club publishes a machine-readable depth chart, and whether any of them agree with each other on the same date.
missing_data: A league-wide official depth feed. Full 32-club depth chart capture.
recommended_path: Treat 'official depth chart' as unavailable. Rank depth explicitly from roster status codes plus published club depth charts, and label every derived rank as *derived*, never as official.
answer: No. https://www.nfl.com/depth-charts/ returns 404 (S13). Depth comes from the clubs' own published chart pages — 30 clubs plus the special-cased Chiefs capture are registered URL-per-club in data/depth-sources.tsv — and every derived rank is labelled derived, never official (D-42; club-chart caveat F10).

question: Are official snap counts published, so a starter's replacement can be measured rather than guessed?
why_it_matters: The only rigorous way to say a backup 'had to replace a starter' is to show the starter's snap share fell and the backup's rose. Without snap counts the claim is narrative, not measurement.
what_we_know: The official injury report tells us who is Out/Doubtful/Questionable but not how many snaps anyone played.
what_we_dont_know: Whether snap counts are available to this project from an official or licensed source.
missing_data: Snap-count data. Not present in this repo and not retrievable from the pages verified here.
blocking: No, but it caps the ceiling on the deficiency model
recommended_path: Mark the deficiency model as specification-only until snap data exists. Do not fabricate snap shares.
answer: Not established: no official snap-count file exists in this repo, which is exactly why the snap-count starter proxy is blocked (D-55, D-30). Until an official snap source covering all 32 clubs is verified (or club-chart coverage reaches 32/32 from 30/32 today), starter/replacement logic rests only on club charts and dated announced-starter evidence.

question: How is the injury report snapped and versioned, given that it changes several times per week?
why_it_matters: A player can be Full on Wednesday and Out on Saturday. If snapshots are not timestamped, any model trained on the report is using information that did not exist at the time — a look-ahead bias that manufactures fake skill.
what_we_know: The Week 10 report captured here (S01) is a single point-in-time snapshot taken 2026-11-14, and it is already partly final: e.g. Sam Darnold is listed Out and a same-page NFL news item confirms he was ruled out.
what_we_dont_know: The exact publication cadence per club, and whether earlier-week versions are archived anywhere official and free.
missing_data: A time series of injury reports. This repo holds one snapshot only.
recommended_path: Store every snapshot with a UTC timestamp and never overwrite. Backfill is impossible; start the series now.
answer: Method settled: each read is captured verbatim under raw/ with a clock-bracketed window (three dated reads: 2026-11-14, 2026-11-16, 2026-11-17), parsed by one shared grammar, its header row-claim asserted against the parser, and published as a delta — latest diff plus the earlier one under history in data/injury_hub_delta.json (D-21). Still open: which dated read a backtest may pin (Q40) and durable hash-pinned storage (D-28).

question: What do the practice and game-status designations officially mean, and can the definitions be quoted from an official source?
why_it_matters: 'Questionable' has a specific league meaning. Treating Doubtful and Questionable as equally likely to play would corrupt any availability model.
what_we_know: The verified pages show four practice states (Full Participation, Limited Participation, Did Not Participate) and four game statuses (Out, Doubtful, Questionable, blank).
what_we_dont_know: The official definition text. The 2017 policy PDF cited everywhere on the web returns 404 from operations.nfl.com (S12), and the operations injury-report landing page also 404s (S14).
missing_data: A retrievable official definition of each designation.
blocking: No, but it is a flagged gap
recommended_path: Record the observed categories as observed, and put the definition gap on the Flagged for Review page rather than paraphrasing a policy we could not retrieve.
answer: Official text supplies labels only — Out/Doubtful/Questionable and the three practice statuses map 1:1 in the capture grammar, and no official percentages exist. The empirical meaning (play rate per designation with confidence intervals, joined to official inactives over several seasons) has not been measured (D-43, D-52), so no outside percentage may be quoted as fact. Clears when a multi-season join of official designations to official inactives yields play rates with confidence intervals.

question: How should the cross-source irregularities found in this repo be handled?
why_it_matters: Two official pages disagree. If the build silently picks one, every downstream number inherits an unstated choice.
what_we_know: Case 1: NFL.com's Week 10 injury page lists Myles Garrett as a Rams LB, while NFL.com's own Next Gen Stats page carries a Rams article titled 'No timeline on Myles Garrett's return post knee surgery', and a separate NFL.com article places Garrett in the Rams defense. Case 2: Aaron Donald is listed as a Did Not Participate on the Rams injury table and NFL.com's player profile shows him active with the Rams, consistent with a same-season NFL.com report that he unretired on Aug. 30 and planned a season debut. Case 3: the injury page header reads 'Week 10 of the 2026 Season' while the article slug for the same week is dated 2026 — consistent — but the Commanders' sideline game is shown as FINAL 24-21 on Nov 12 while the injury page still lists them.
what_we_dont_know: Whether these are data-entry errors at the source, stale cached rows, or genuinely correct and our reading is wrong.
missing_data: An authoritative roster-move log to reconcile against.
recommended_path: Do not reconcile by hand. Publish the discrepancy verbatim with both source links on the Flagged for Review page and leave the affected cells as captured.
answer: Published, never suppressed: every cross-source irregularity becomes a row on flagged.html with detail, action and source links (66 flags today; F61 was corrected 2026-11-17 after re-reading the official pages; F53 records the row-count discrepancy). Per the brief, flagged items do not block a merge, and a cell that cannot be confirmed from an official source stays blank and flagged rather than filled (tools/checkrows.py rules 1-4).

question: What sample size would make a strategy's result distinguishable from luck, and how long is one NFL season?
why_it_matters: A season is short. At roughly 272 regular-season games, even a genuinely good model produces results well inside noise over a few weeks. Claiming skill from a 20-bet record is arithmetic, not opinion: the confidence interval swallows the edge.
what_we_know: A 2026 regular season runs 18 weeks; Week 10 is in progress and the league calendar shows Week 18 on Jan 9-10, 2027, with Super Bowl LXI on Feb 14, 2027 (S05). Division standings confirm clubs have played 8-9 games (S02).
what_we_dont_know: The effect size any strategy will actually achieve, which is what determines the sample needed.
missing_data: Historical graded results to estimate variance.
recommended_path: State a minimum sample gate up front, pre-register it, and refuse to rank a strategy until it clears the gate. Use a binomial or bootstrap interval, not a bare win rate.
answer: Answered per strategy by the removal-of-luck panels: skill means the 95% lower bound of hit rate clears the vig-adjusted break-even hurdle after a multiplicity adjustment for every trial run (the register's best ROI entry is rejected on exactly this: 936 settled bets, 51.07% lower bound vs 52.38% hurdle — data/luck_panel_signal.json). The open half: which number becomes the leaderboard's standing qualification bar (Q43).

question: How is 'luck removed' defined operationally, rather than as a slogan?
why_it_matters: The brief asks to remove luck. That needs a testable definition or it becomes an untestable claim.
what_we_know: Three measurable proxies exist with data we can actually get: (a) calibration — do 60% predictions win 60% of the time; (b) closing-line value — did the fair value move toward our number; (c) persistence — does the edge hold out of sample and across seasons.
what_we_dont_know: Which proxy the user will accept as the definition.
missing_data: A benchmark price feed for the CLV test.
recommended_path: Adopt all three as separate gates. A strategy must pass calibration first; CLV and persistence are additional. Never average them into one score.
answer: Operationally: benchmark-relative skill with uncertainty — the luck-removed edge (hit-rate lower bound minus hurdle), a game-cluster lower bound, a multiplicity adjustment, and control baselines, with PROVEN/NOT PROVEN verdicts published on removal-of-luck.html from data/luck_panel_signal.json and data/luck_panel.json. Win rate and ROI may be displayed but can never set a rank (D-37; season-long ROI ranking rejected, D-64).

question: How are correlation values computed for parlays and prop combos, and from what joint data?
why_it_matters: Parlay pricing depends entirely on the joint distribution. If two legs are positively correlated, multiplying their probabilities underprices the parlay and misstates the edge.
what_we_know: Correlation requires repeated joint observations of the same pairing. Team-level scoring is available from official standings (S03), so team totals can supply joint observations.
what_we_dont_know: Whether player-level joint outcomes can be assembled at all from official sources at the depth needed, and how many observations per pair are required.
missing_data: Player game logs sufficient to estimate pairwise prop correlations.
blocking: Yes — for parlay and combo products
recommended_path: Start correlations at the team-total level where data exists. For player props, publish the method and mark correlations blank until the joint sample is adequate.
answer: From official rows only: data/correlations_official.json computes every value from rows transcribed from official league sources (S01/S03/S52) with n published per value (e.g. C-A1: n=32, r=0.8781), and engine/corr_official.py refuses non-official source ids — third-party measures stay in their own labelled registers (R27, D-07). A pair becomes usable for parlays/combos only through the joint-evidence gate (D-35).

question: What counts as out-of-sample, and how is the holdout protected from repeated peeking?
why_it_matters: If the same data is used to choose a model and to score it, the score is optimistic. Repeatedly checking the holdout while tuning destroys it.
what_we_know: Official data is organised by season and week, so strict time-based splits are natural: train on earlier weeks, test on later ones.
what_we_dont_know: Whether enough seasons are available to the project for a meaningful multi-season holdout.
missing_data: Multiple completed seasons of the same official fields.
recommended_path: Walk-forward validation only, no random shuffling. Freeze the holdout in a separate file and log every access to it.
answer: Chronologically, frozen before scoring: the ablation corpus splits train 1999-2019 / validation 2020-2021 / final holdout 2022-2025 (scored once, after freezing) with 2026 excluded as in-progress (data/ablations.json design.splits; D-69). Pre-registration (D-66, D-68) fixes rule text, sample window and gates in git before the evaluation window opens; a scored holdout is never reopened.

question: What exactly is rewarded on the leaderboard, and is anything of value actually paid out?
why_it_matters: The brief asks for rewards for top strategies. If rewards are not defined, the leaderboard ranks on whatever metric happens to be convenient, and that metric will be gamed.
what_we_know: Rewards can be defined entirely in-repo as ranking position and a badge, with no monetary component.
what_we_dont_know: Whether the user intends real money, and if so the legal and tax position.
missing_data: A decision from the user on any monetary component.
recommended_path: Default to a non-monetary points-based leaderboard. If money is ever considered, that requires a jurisdiction-specific legal and tax review first — see Q14.
answer: What is ranked: luck-adjusted skill computed from a sealed, walk-forward bet log, gates first, with rewards conditional on passing them (data/leaderboard.json design; D-37). What is rewarded in value: nothing today — no payout, bankroll or currency mechanism exists anywhere in the repo (cf. economics OQ-02), so the reward design remains an owner decision.

question: Does producing lines and publishing them raise any legal issue, and does the responsible regulator need to be identified?
why_it_matters: Publishing prices or running a contest with entry fees touches gambling regulation in the United States, and the rules differ by state. The user is located in Mexico City, which adds a second jurisdiction question.
what_we_know: Nothing in this repo constitutes a bet, a bookmaking service, or an offer to wager. No money changes hands.
what_we_dont_know: Whether a public leaderboard with prizes would be treated as a contest of skill or of chance in any relevant jurisdiction, and which regulator applies.
missing_data: Legal review. Regulator sources were not verified in this session.
blocking: Only if money or prizes are introduced
recommended_path: Keep the site informational and non-monetary. Put the open legal question on the Flagged for Review page and do not assert a legal conclusion.
answer: Not answerable from data or official sources: the legal/regulator question (Q14, SG11) has had no counsel input. Before any decision: the owner's jurisdiction and whether any stake is real (OQ-02). Nothing published here is legal advice or evidence of compliance.

question: Which Week 10 games have no injury report in the captured snapshot, and is that because the report is not yet due?
why_it_matters: The snapshot covers 28 of 32 clubs. Anyone averaging 'injuries per team' over the wrong denominator gets a biased number.
what_we_know: Four clubs are absent from the Week 10 injury tables: CHI, DEN, TB and PHI. By contrast, every one of the 28 clubs in the snapshot is one of the 28 clubs appearing in the Week 10 schedule capture (S04), which has 14 games.
what_we_dont_know: Whether those four clubs have a bye in Week 10 or their reports simply were not yet posted at capture time.
missing_data: An official 2026 bye-week table.
recommended_path: Report the count as 28 of 32 clubs present, never as a league total, and flag the four missing clubs as an open question.
answer: None in the current captures: the canonical table holds 345 rows across all 28 clubs that played Week 10 — every one of the 14 games has both teams' rows (data/injuries.tsv, S01) — and each of the three dated hub reads prints a section for each of the 14 games. The gaps behind this question belonged to the stale 254-row pages, replaced by the re-capture (D-48; F53 keeps the count discrepancy on record).

question: How are 'not injury related' entries handled so they do not pollute an injury signal?
why_it_matters: The report mixes injury with rest and personal absence. Counting 'resting player' as an injury inflates the injury rate and misclassifies the reason a starter is missing.
what_we_know: The captured report contains explicit non-injury entries: 'Not injury related - resting player' (two Jaguars) and 'Not injury related - personal matter' (one Texan). These are recorded verbatim.
what_we_dont_know: Whether other absences with an empty injury field are also non-injury.
missing_data: A definitive presence/absence reason per player.
recommended_path: Never bucket an empty injury field as an injury. Tag non-injury rows explicitly and exclude them from injury-rate denominators.
answer: Carried verbatim from the league's own text and explicitly marked: the per-team availability build publishes a nonInjury count per club and its net-injury rule excludes rows the league marks 'Not injury related' (scripts/build_availability_g.py, netInjuryRule). They never enter the injury count silently.

question: Which additional inputs are officially obtainable, and which require a licensed vendor?
why_it_matters: Weather, travel, rest days and officiating crew all plausibly move a line. If any of them requires a paid feed, it belongs on the open-questions list rather than in the model.
what_we_know: Official and free: local forecasts from the National Weather Service (S11), schedules with kickoff times (S04), and tracking-derived metrics from Next Gen Stats (S10).
what_we_dont_know: Officiating crew assignments, exact rest-day differentials, and any sourced stadium/roof database.
missing_data: Crew assignments; a roof and surface registry.
recommended_path: Use only the free official inputs first. Add each new input only after the base model is validated, one at a time, so its contribution can be measured.
answer: Obtained official inputs are enumerated: 83 registered sources, 75 VERIFIED, each with URL and capture date (data/sources.tsv). Licensed vendors are not among them — money/contract items sit in the missing-data register as NOT-ATTEMPTED. Which to license (opening prices above all: Q21/Q30) is an owner decision.

question: How does an automated pipeline stay within acceptable use of official sites?
why_it_matters: The brief requires no manual input, so scheduled fetching is implied. Hammering league or club sites can get the project blocked and is not a lawful-by-default practice.
what_we_know: All captures here were single page loads, and the data volume is small.
what_we_dont_know: The terms of use and robots policy of nfl.com and the 32 club sites, which were not reviewed in this session.
missing_data: A terms-of-use review.
recommended_path: Read the terms before automating. Until then, treat capture as manual-triggered, low-rate, and cached.
answer: No terms review exists, so no defensible yes/no. Practice so far: a handful of clock-bracketed dated reads per page with verbatim capture (raw/ headers), not continuous scraping. Before any cadence is automated (D-53) the owner must accept an acceptable-use position or name counsel to check (pairs Q14, OQ-02).

question: How is a strategy's edge tested against a naive baseline, so that the model gets credit only for what it actually adds?
why_it_matters: A model that reproduces 'good teams beat bad teams' is not skill. Without a baseline, any strategy looks impressive against zero.
what_we_know: Official standings give season-to-date scoring and records for all 32 clubs (S03), enough to build a simple baseline such as a points-differential rating.
what_we_dont_know: The baseline the user considers fair.
missing_data: A stated baseline.
recommended_path: Every strategy must beat a named, published baseline out of sample, or it is not ranked. Publish the baseline alongside the strategy.
answer: Measured against vig-adjusted break-even hurdles plus a market control: betting every home team at the close runs 5,067 settled bets at -5.19% ROI — pure house margin (data/luck_panel_signal.json control_baseline). The random-picks and favourites-only controls the brief names are not yet in every run (D-56) — the open half is the owner's adoption of those two controls into every leaderboard run; the addition itself is mechanical.

question: Who owns each task when several sessions run at once, and what happens on a stale claim?
why_it_matters: Shared files edited by two sessions create silent overwrites and duplicated work.
what_we_know: COORDINATION.md in this repo defines the board, the status vocabulary, a 60-minute stale-claim takeover rule, and a rule that shared outputs are changed only by the final integration session.
what_we_dont_know: Whether other sessions are actually active.
missing_data: None.
recommended_path: Keep the board current. Log every claim and every handoff with a UTC timestamp.
answer: Written in COORDINATION.md: read the board first; claim by pushing session id and file scope immediately; never start a claimed task; keep scopes non-overlapping on session branches; small frequent commits with pull --rebase; log cross-scope requests instead of editing; a claim idle over 60 minutes with no commits is open for takeover with a logged handoff; 'done' requires sources, verification and irregularities recorded. This session pushed its claim before any other work.

question: What approved source will supply OPENING prices for every market we originate?
why_it_matters: The price-snapshot store records the open field, but every open cell is blank: without a source there is no honest number, and without the number closing-line value cannot be computed from the open.
what_we_know: The store (data/price_snapshots.json) has the fields and the discipline. Closing prices come from the pinned nflverse capture (S47). No official league source prices NFL markets (F23).
what_we_dont_know: Whether a licensed line-history feed will be purchased or approved.
missing_data: Licensed opening + closing line history (GAP-01).
recommended_path: Option A (SG21): buy licensed history. Interim (SG20): snapshot the market's open at the moment we publish our own line, prospectively from Week 11.
answer: No approved source. The price-snapshot store exists (D-01 store done) but opening values are blocked: no opening-price source has been chosen (D-01 'blocked (values)'; Q30), and the one captured opening line (2021 single-book) stays quarantined (Q37). Clearing: a named source, cadence and redistribution terms recorded in the register.

question: Where will moneyline opening and closing prices come from?
why_it_matters: Requirement R21 says every market we originate, and the moneyline is one of the three mandated markets. Its price cells are all blank today.
what_we_know: closing_lines.csv holds third-party moneyline prices for 2006-2025 only; the Week 10 2026 board captures spread and total but no moneyline.
what_we_dont_know: Any approved 2026 moneyline capture source.
missing_data: 2026 moneyline prices (open and close).
recommended_path: Extend the capture pipeline to record moneyline odds alongside spread/total, or approve a feed that carries them.
answer: Same gap as Q21 — no approved source for moneyline open/close. The store keeps what the labelled feed provides (close, when provided) and leaves the rest blank; blocked on the Q30 decision (source, cadence, redistribution).

question: May third-party market prices back published difference and staking numbers, or must those cells stay blank?
why_it_matters: Requirement R24 demands a market-line column and a difference column; the standing verification rule says values without an official source are left blank. Both cannot hold unless the owner picks a policy. This is the open F-11 decision, now unavoidable.
what_we_know: The computed research layer already publishes third-party-derived values with labels; the root site's footer promised no price figures without official support, amended in this sprint to describe the THIRD_PARTY badge.
what_we_dont_know: The owner's preference among the three options below.
missing_data: None - this is a decision, not a data gap.
recommended_path: A: publish with THIRD_PARTY badge + flag until C is affordable; B switches every market cell to blank with one edit; C needs Q21's purchase.
answer: Interim rule in force, ratification open: third-party-derived cells publish only with explicit labels/flags (market_provenance 'third-party ... flagged'; THIRD_PARTY badges on the boards). Promoting them to headline difference/staking numbers is the reserved owner call (Q32; D-20).

question: Are the demotion-gate thresholds (100-bet window, 25-unit drawdown, p<0.10, 300-bet re-promotion) the rules to adopt?
why_it_matters: The gate defines when a live strategy goes back to paper. Wrong thresholds either strand dead strategies live or kill recovering ones.
what_we_know: Defaults are published as constructor arguments in engine/demotion.py and rendered verbatim as G-14.
what_we_dont_know: The owner's risk appetite for false demotions vs slow demotions.
missing_data: None - a rule choice.
recommended_path: Adopt as written for the first season (SG22) and revisit after 300 settled bets of live history.
answer: Numbers exist and are frozen, but they are not the brief's sketch: data/market/demotion_config.json (2026-11-14) fixes a 200-bet window (min 60), D1 lower-bound fail < 0, D2 slope band 0.4-1.6, D3 caps 0.35/0.30/0.35, D4 price gap <= 5%, <= 2 demotions per season, reprobe >= 150 paper bets; G-16 demotes live -> paper automatically. Ratifying these instead of the 100-bet / 25-unit / p<0.10 sketch is the open half (Q33, SG17).

question: What staking plans may entries use at all, now that rank counts signal only?
why_it_matters: Rewards must not pay on staking luck (R25), but staking still determines real-world results and drawdowns. The allowed plans need to be fixed before entries open.
what_we_know: The leaderboard reports a staking block separately; the engine computes both from one log.
what_we_dont_know: Whether flat-only, capped fractional Kelly, or author-defined stakes will be permitted.
missing_data: None - a rule choice.
recommended_path: Flat 1 unit for the scored sample; optional separate staking report capped at 2 units (matches the exposure cap in GateConfig).
answer: Rank-side settled: staking can never affect a rank (signal/staking split, D-05), and each entry carries two-sided change-of-mind fields (D-17). The allowed plan list is not: Kelly-style sizing waits on bankroll, unit and jurisdiction (OQ-02), so paper entries run flat units by convention until the owner sets rules.

question: When do we fit the fair model's coefficients out-of-sample instead of publishing the naive baseline?
why_it_matters: The naive baseline (strength = (PF-PA)/G, /2 convention) is deliberately crude. Publishing a fitted model too early invites overfitting; too late leaves edge on the table.
what_we_know: models.json attaches the estimator (maximise out-of-sample log-loss, never tune PnL). Coefficients today are computed from 137 official 2026 games (F29).
what_we_dont_know: When enough official seasons will be captured to fit and validate honestly.
missing_data: Multi-season official results feed (today: 2026 weeks 1-10 only).
recommended_path: Keep the baseline published; schedule the first refit after two full official seasons are captured.
answer: Today no fitted coefficients populate published lines: output is the frozen pre-registered baseline fl1-elo-v1 (model_version column) with its calibration report (n=5,336 games; mean signed error -0.77 pts, MAE 2.89 pts vs close). Fitting starts only after acceptance criteria are frozen (Q31, open) and the switch itself is pre-registered (D-66, D-68).

question: What verified source will confirm WHO actually replaces a starter on the field?
why_it_matters: Replacement depth today is chart-based: the club's own depth chart says who is next. Snap counts would confirm who actually took the snaps.
what_we_know: Club depth charts are self-published and labelled unofficial (S07/S08/S16-S46); the official report says who is Out. data/replacement_depth.tsv joins the two without asserting playing time.
what_we_dont_know: Any verified snap-count feed.
missing_data: Snap counts per game (GAP-05 family).
recommended_path: Add a snap-count source once one is verified; until then label every replacement as chart-based.
answer: Route (a) stands at 30/32 clubs: per-club chart pages registered URL-per-row (data/depth-sources.tsv) plus 11 dated, quoted announced-starter rows (data/announced_starters.csv) on a point-in-time ledger. question: Which officially sourced correlation pairs should be captured every week to grow n?

question: Which of the two parallel implementations of R21-R28 becomes canonical for each requirement?

question: Which licensed source will supply OPENING prices, at what capture cadence, and under what redistribution terms?  (pairs with SG30)

question: What acceptance criteria must a fitted fair-line model meet before its numbers populate the Origination Board?  (pairs with SG34; see flag F20)
why_it_matters: The board's fair column is blank by design until a model exists (F19). Without pre-accepted criteria, a model could be accepted because its numbers look good rather than because they beat a baseline.

what_we_dont_know: The out-of-sample bar: log-loss versus the naive baseline, calibration tolerance, and how wide the published uncertainty band must be.
missing_data: A pre-registered acceptance threshold set.
recommended_path: Pre-register in one commit: the model must beat the naive margin baseline on out-of-sample log loss, publish an uncertainty band with every fair line, and be sealed (hashed) before kickoff. Reject otherwise.

question: May third-party-derived values be published as sourced on the headline registers, or must every published value resolve to an official source?  (pairs with SG19)
why_it_matters: This decides whether correlations, market numbers and historical results can ever fill in. The strict rule keeps registers blank where no official source exists; the loose rule risks a reader trusting a number the league never published.

what_we_dont_know: Your decision.
missing_data: None - a policy choice.
recommended_path: Keep headline registers official-only and keep labelled third-party appendices as they are. The cost of the strict rule is visible blank cells; the cost of the loose rule is invisible trust leakage. Revisit only with a licensed feed (Q21).

question: What numeric thresholds do demotion rules D1-D3 use, and when are they frozen?  (pairs with SG17 and SG31)

The brief's sketch (100-bet window, 25-unit drawdown, p<0.10, 300-bet re-promotion) was not adopted verbatim — confirming the implemented numbers is the open half (pairs SG17).

question: Should the verified results feed backfill 1999-2025 from third-party rows (labelled) so backtests have history?  (pairs with SG32)

question: Should the snapshot store accept a fourth phase value for prices whose vintage the publisher never stated, or stay close-only?

If the store cannot hold them, the store is a 2006-2018 closing-lines table and every current-season origination number lives outside it; if it holds them under a label meaning 'intermediate', the ledger asserts a provenance nobody has.

recommended_path: Add UNDOCUMENTED to the phase CHECK and keep the strict provenance columns (source_url, source_record_id, line_origin_version) mandatory, so widening the enum does not widen the trust boundary. Then this session's loader writes the full 78,410-row ledger instead of 20,490 rows.
answer: Open — whether the store's phase enum gains a value for prices whose vintage the publisher never stated is a schema/owner decision. Interim: such rows are labelled CLOSE_OR_UNDOCUMENTED in the backtest bench and the 2021 opening line stays quarantined (Q37). NOTE: Q45 duplicates this question verbatim (merge re-issue) — see F67; folding them together belongs to SG47.

question: What price basis should a published ROI use when the feed carries a line but no odds?
why_it_matters: A quarter of the backtest log is priced at an assumed -110 because the games feed publishes spread and total numbers without payout for those games. ROI on an assumed price is a model statistic, not a market result, and it will be read as the latter if it is not labelled.

what_we_dont_know: Whether the site should show ROI for the unpriced subset at all, or restrict the headline ROI to posted-price rows and show the rest as points-beat only.

blocking: no - the choice is presentational, the data does not change
recommended_path: Publish both: headline ROI restricted to posted-price bets, with the full-log figure in the same table under an 'assumed price' column. Never blend them into one number.

The final headline basis waits on the price-source decisions (Q21, Q30).

question: Is the 2021 single-book opening line worth a published movement table, or should it stay quarantined?

Nothing is inferred into the blank; ratifying this behaviour as the standing rule is a formality.

question: Should a D4 integrity trigger block a merge, or only block promotion?

question: Which dated read of the injury report is the canonical pre-kickoff snapshot for backtests?
why_it_matters: This session proved the report moves: two reads two days apart differ by two rows and 32 fields. A backtest that trains on the Monday read has seen designations that did not exist before kickoff, which is lookahead leakage and will flatter any availability strategy.

The canonical injuries.tsv stays on read 1 while later reads publish as deltas. Choosing first-pre-kickoff vs latest-before-kickoff is an owner decision that sets backtest reproducibility.

question: Should the leaderboard adopt the removal-of-luck numbers as its qualification bar?
why_it_matters: The leaderboard ranks strategies. Without a sample-size bar it will rank whoever had the best short run. The panel shows that 785 independent decisions are needed to detect a 5pp edge at all, and 1,211 once six strategies are tried.

answer: Open — both luck panels publish exactly the numbers such a bar would use (edge lower bound vs hurdle, multiplicity-adjusted verdicts, control baselines). Adopting them as the leaderboard's standing qualification rule is an owner choice; if adopted, write it into the leaderboard register as a frozen gate (D-66, D-68).

A workable rule to ratify: auto-promote only when a fresh official read prints every game FINAL and all V-checks pass — then it can run inside the weekly refresh (SG49).
